narrative: Your application was denied because the model estimated a 74.7% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. In practical terms, the review process treated that as a high risk, so admission was not offered. The strongest factor behind that estimate was your third-year class standing: you were in the second decile, well below the average of about 5.8 among admitted students, and this was the single largest push toward failure. Your first-year standing also mattered: at the third decile, compared with an admitted-student average of 6.0, it was the third most influential factor and again pushed the prediction toward failure. Between those two, your LSAT score was the second most important factor, but it worked in your favor: at 38, slightly above the admitted-student average of about 37.2, it pushed toward passing. The denial therefore reflects concern concentrated in your law-school grades, especially your later-year standing, rather than in your LSAT. Next, you should meet with an academic advisor to understand the third-year grade decline, consider whether additional coursework or a delayed application can show improved academic performance, and prepare a brief addendum explaining any context. If you reapply, seek programs that review applicants holistically and ask what evidence they would need to offset the academic concern.
